title: Objects, Fields, and Records
summary: Use a small vehicle catalogue to distinguish the shape of information from individual stored items.
prerequisites: J01–J04: the business example, your learning org, and basic navigation.
learningObjectives: Distinguish objects, fields, records, and values.
Read the starter's principal API names.
Explain why an event needs its own record.

sections.heading: One catalogue, several vehicles
body: Northstar needs to keep information about vehicles it can offer customers. An object describes a kind of information stored in Salesforce. Our example is Vehicle. A field describes one property of that kind of item, such as Model or Status. A record stores the values for one particular vehicle. Two physical vehicles require two records, even if their models are identical.

Imagine a table with Model, VIN, and Status as column headings. Each row describes a vehicle. The table is a useful analogy for an object, the column headings resemble fields, and the rows resemble records. The analogy helps you read the structure; it does not mean Salesforce is simply a spreadsheet or that every application must be designed as one large table.

callouts.text: An object describes a category. A record represents one member of that category.

sections.heading: Separate a field definition from its value
body: The course starter uses Vehicle__c, with Model__c, VIN__c, and Status__c. The __c suffix identifies a custom object or field in these API names. An API name is the identifier used by configuration files and code; the visible label is the name a user reads. For now, recognize the distinction without memorizing every naming rule.

Model__c is a text field. 'City EV' is one possible value. Status__c is a picklist: a field offering a defined set of choices. In the starter those choices are Available, Reserved, and Unavailable. VIN__c is text with a uniqueness constraint in this educational schema. A constraint is a rule the system applies to stored data. We use fictional identifiers, not real vehicle or customer information.

When a third vehicle arrives, Anna creates another record. When Oleg decides every vehicle needs a mileage value, the team considers adding a field. Adding the field does not automatically discover each vehicle's mileage. Someone must supply the values or define a reliable source. Confusing these two changes leads to duplicate objects and missing business information.

callouts.text: Point to a field name and a field value in your drawing. They should not be the same concept.

sections.heading: Introduce relationships carefully
body: A test drive is a separate event involving a vehicle and a customer. Northstar may run several test drives for the same vehicle on different days. Copying the entire vehicle description into every event would make updates difficult. A relationship instead points from one record to another, allowing the event to identify its vehicle.

The starter Test_Drive__c object includes Vehicle__c, a relationship to a vehicle; Customer__c, a relationship to Contact; Scheduled_At__c, a date and time; and Status__c, the event's status. The vehicle's availability and the test drive's progress answer different questions. A vehicle can be Available while one earlier test drive is Completed. Do not merge those status fields into one shared meaning.

You do not need to configure the relationship yet. J09 explains its behaviour. Today's task is to describe which information belongs to a vehicle and which belongs to a particular appointment, and to notice why one item can participate in many events.

callouts.text: These are the course starter's design choices, not a universal automotive data model.

steps.title: Create two paper records
steps.instruction: Draw two vehicle cards with different fictional VIN values and the same field names.
steps.expected: The cards share a structure but identify different vehicles.

steps.title: Add one event
steps.instruction: Draw a test-drive card and an arrow to one vehicle card.
steps.expected: The event refers to the selected vehicle rather than duplicating the whole catalogue.

steps.title: Classify a change
steps.instruction: Describe adding another vehicle, then adding a mileage field.
steps.expected: You distinguish a data change from a structure change.

exercise.title: Model the smallest useful catalogue
exercise.brief: Create a diagram containing two vehicles and three test-drive events.
steps: Write the field names once for each object.
Give each vehicle a distinct fictional identifier.
Connect two events to the same vehicle on different days.
acceptance: Objects, fields, values, and records are labelled correctly.
Vehicle status is distinct from test-drive status.

knowledgeCheck.question: Is City EV a field?
knowledgeCheck.answer: No. It is a possible value of the Model field.

knowledgeCheck.question: Does every physical car need a different custom object?
knowledgeCheck.answer: No. It needs a separate record in the Vehicle object.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why separate a test drive from a vehicle?
knowledgeCheck.answer: A vehicle can take part in several events with different customers, dates, and outcomes.

recap: Distinguish objects, fields, records, and values.
Read the starter's principal API names.
Explain why an event needs its own record.
